hints: Start from the two labels you are given - G1 phase at the top and telophase near the bottom. What large blocks of the cycle do these belong to?

Remember what happens between G1 and mitosis - DNA must be copied and then checked, so think S for synthesis and G2 for growth. For mitosis, think of the chromosome journey: condensing, lining up, pulling apart, then reforming nuclei.

The right-hand bracket groups the first three rows together and the next four rows together. Use this to name the two main phases: interphase and mitosis, and place S, G2 and prophase, metaphase, anaphase in order.
walkthrough:
Sort Interphase First**
Think of interphase as the preparation time before division. It starts with G1 phase for normal growth and protein synthesis. Next comes S phase where DNA is replicated to form sister chromatids. Then G2 phase for further growth and checking DNA replication. Those three together are called interphase.

Sort Mitosis In Chromosome Order**
Mitosis moves chromosomes in a logical sequence. Prophase: chromosomes condense and become visible. Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the spindle equator. Anaphase: sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles. Telophase: nuclear envelopes reform. That is the order given by the spindle story.

Put The Whole Cycle Together**
From top to bottom: G1 phase, S phase, G2 phase (all interphase), then prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase (all mitosis), then cytokinesis to split the cytoplasm into two genetically identical daughter cells.
Final answer: Top bracket = interphase: G1 phase, S phase, G2 phase. Bottom bracket = mitosis: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, followed by cytokinesis.

hints: Match each drug to when it acts. One blocks building of DNA bases, the other blocks pulling of chromosomes - which stage needs each?

If DNA cannot be copied in S phase, later events cannot start. If the spindle cannot work, early events still happen but lining up and separating cannot happen. Use this to decide tick or cross for each column.
walkthrough:
Work Through Vincristine - Spindle Poison**
Vincristine binds spindle microtubules, so it only hits mitosis. DNA replication in S phase is normal, so S-phase completes. The cell can still enter prophase and condense chromosomes. But without a working spindle, chromosomes cannot line up at the equator in metaphase and sister chromatids cannot be pulled to opposite poles in anaphase. So the pattern is tick, tick, cross, cross.

Work Through 5-Fluorouracil - DNA Building Block Blocker**
5-fluorouracil prevents synthesis of thymine nucleotides, so DNA cannot be replicated. That means S phase cannot complete. Because DNA is not copied, checkpoints stop the cycle and the cell will not proceed to prophase, will not line up chromosomes and will not separate chromatids. It is likely to undergo apoptosis. So the pattern is cross, cross, cross, cross.

Final answer: Vincristine: S-phase completes ✓, cell enters prophase ✓, chromosomes line up X, sister chromatids move to poles X. 5-fluorouracil: S-phase completes X, cell enters prophase X, chromosomes line up X, sister chromatids move to poles X.

walkthrough: Current-syllabus full-credit observation route: Compare the supplied smear with normal blood cells. There are many more lymphocytes, their normal large distinct nuclei are not apparent, and distinct monocytes cannot be identified. These are three separate accepted observations in the official scheme. The historical explanations below add accepted disease-specific alternatives, but those mechanisms are not needed for this image-based route.

Describe The Smear - Too Many White Cells**
In a healthy smear you would see mostly small pale red blood cells with very few darker lymphocytes scattered between. In Fig. 6.1 the field is packed with large dark-staining lymphocytes, with only a few small red blood cells visible underneath. That shows a greatly increased number of lymphocytes due to uncontrolled mitosis.

Describe The Lymphocytes - Large And Immature**
Healthy lymphocytes are small with a large dark nucleus filling most of the cell. The leukaemia cells in Fig. 6.1 are larger and look immature and not fully developed, with abnormal nuclear appearance. They have divided too quickly to differentiate properly.

Add Function - Non-Functional Cells**
Because they are immature, these leukaemia lymphocytes are non-functional and cannot carry out normal immune responses such as antibody production. That is why leukaemia impairs immunity despite the high white cell count.

Final answer: Blood smear differences: many more lymphocytes than normal, crowded field with few visible red blood cells. Lymphocyte differences: larger, immature / not fully developed, lack normal large nucleus structure and are non-functional in immunity.
